one_liner: Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03 C compiled to WASM through a Rust wasm-bindgen shim; beats astronomy-engine on Moon positions only (1.44x).
what_it_does: Exposes a small subset of the Swiss Ephemeris C API (swe_calc_ut, swe_julday, swe_revjul, swe_fixstar_ut, swe_pheno_ut, swe_set_topo, swe_set_sid_mode, swe_get_ayanamsa_ut, swe_get_planet_name, swe_sidtime) to Deno, Node, Bun and browsers from one WASM module, published on JSR, npm and crates.io. swe_calc_ut returns a JS object {longitude, latitude, distance, speed_long, speed_lat, speed_dist, rc_flags} in ecliptic-of-date coordinates. The API is Swiss Ephemeris's, not astronomy-engine's, so switching means rewriting call sites.
how_it_is_fast: There is no algorithmic trick: the C library is compiled with clang for wasm32-unknown-unknown (build.rs sets warnings and the target but no -O flag; the libc is replaced by Rust shims over libm and a header-tagged malloc), and calls go through wasm-bindgen. The Moon win comes from running compiled C for the lunar series instead of JIT-compiled JavaScript. On cheap calls the binding cost dominates: each swe_calc_ut builds its result with Object::new plus seven Reflect::set imports across the WASM/JS boundary, which is why the Sun rows lose to pure JS.
when_to_use: You already use Swiss Ephemeris conventions (swe_* calls, SE_/SEFLG_ constants, sidereal modes, ayanamsa) and need them in a browser or Deno/Node without a native addon.
Moon-heavy batch work (e.g. lunar tables) where the README's Deno bench shows about 182,000 vs 126,000 iter/s over astronomy-engine.

Astrology-style output (apparent ecliptic longitude/latitude with daily speeds) where Moshier-level precision is enough; swemmoon.c quotes at most 7 arcsec longitude error for the Moshier Moon over -3000 to +3000.
AGPL-3.0-compatible projects, or projects holding a Swiss Ephemeris Professional License.
when_not_to_use: Sun and other cheap per-call positions: the README itself shows astronomy-engine faster (about 577,000 vs 319,000 ops/s in Chrome, 434,000 vs 178,000 in Deno).
When you need the SE1 file ephemerides or JPL files: fopen, fread and stat are stubbed (src/lib.rs) and swe_set_ephe_path is not exported, so every SEFLG_SWIEPH call silently falls back to Moshier.
Fixed stars: swe_fixstar_ut needs sefstars.txt, which can never be opened in this build (per source reading, not run).
Closed-source or permissively licensed products: the MIT label covers only the wrapper; the bundled Swiss Ephemeris is AGPL-3.0 or commercial.
Production use needing maturity: 4 stars, 26 commits all from 2026-01-06 to 2026-01-12, tests that only range-check the Sun longitude (275-285 degrees) and Moon latitude.

integration.form: module (JSR @fusionstrings/swisseph-wasm 0.1.5, npm, crates.io crate; browser build with the WASM inlined)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (WASM plus wasm-bindgen glue); build needs Rust with wasm32-unknown-unknown, clang/LLVM with a wasm32 target, Deno and @deno/wasmbuild ^0.21.0
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024 (1.85+), wasm-bindgen 0.2.106, Deno 2.x for build and tests; runtime: any WebAssembly host (Deno, Node, Bun, browsers)
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly runtime with JS glue
integration.thread_safety: not documented; Swiss Ephemeris keeps global state (the swed struct with per-planet save areas, topo and sidereal settings), so treat each instance as single-threaded and one per worker

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the numbers (per source reading of src/lib.rs and vendored sweph.c 2.10.03, not run): the benchmarks request SEFLG_SWIEPH, but fopen returns NULL, so each call first tries the file path, falls back to Moshier, and then swe_calc_ut sees the returned ephemeris flag differ from the requested one and recomputes with a new delta T. The save-area cache never hits because the saved flags (MOSEPH) never equal the requested ones (SWIEPH). Every measured iteration therefore does two Moshier computations; requesting SEFLG_MOSEPH would likely be faster, and the README's 'more accurate' claim describes Moshier, not the SE1 files.

The fallback is silent: the C stubs make sprintf write an empty string and printf/fprintf no-ops, so Swiss Ephemeris warnings and error texts (including 'not found in PATH ... using Moshier') come back blank. Check rc_flags & 4 (SEFLG_MOSEPH) yourself. qsort is a no-op, bsearch returns NULL and atof/atoi/sscanf return 0, so any code path that parses or sorts data is broken.

build.rs defines NO_MOSHIER with the comment 'Use JPL ephemeris only', but neither the vendored sweph.c nor sweph.h references that macro, so it does nothing: Moshier is the only ephemeris that can run.

The workloads differ: Swiss Ephemeris returns apparent ecliptic-of-date coordinates with speeds, while astronomy-engine GeoVector returns a J2000 equatorial vector without velocity. comparison.ts also parses a Date string inside every astronomy-engine iteration, deno_throughput.ts warms up only astronomy-engine, every row uses one fixed date (2000-01-01 12:00 UT), and no CPU, Deno, Chrome or compiler flags are stated.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No astronomy siblings are catalogued; the closest pattern is hash-wasm (C compiled to WASM behind a JS API). Unlike hash-wasm, this one wins only on its heavier call (Moon) and loses on light calls, so use it for Swiss Ephemeris API parity rather than speed.
verified_claims_summary: The first-party README tables (no hardware or versions) show swe_calc_ut for the Moon at about 182,000 iter/s vs astronomy-engine 2.1.19 GeoVector at about 126,000 iter/s in deno bench (1.44x). For the Sun it loses: about 319,000 vs 577,000 ops/s in Chrome and 178,000 vs 434,000 in Deno, with 100,000 iterations timed by performance.now(). All rows are one fixed date, and the WASM side runs the Moshier fallback twice per call.
status_note: A one-week project (26 commits, 2026-01-06 to 2026-01-12) with no activity since and a single open self-PR, so it is dormant rather than active. Usability is mixed: the wrapper is MIT, but shipping the WASM binary carries Swiss Ephemeris AGPL-3.0 or commercial terms.
